## Introduction

*RiboseQC* analyses Ribo-seq data [1] for each read length, in the genomic
regions where the reads map (CDS, UTRs, introns, non-coding RNAs and
intergenic regions) and in each compartment of the cell: the nuclear genome,
and the circular genomes of organelles such as mitochondria and chloroplasts.
It calculates the P-site offset of each read length, selects the read lengths
whose reads show the reading frame, gives their P-sites, and creates an HTML
report that compares samples [2].

This vignette runs the two steps of an analysis on the small example data
included in the package:

1. `prepare_annotation_files()`: parse the annotation and link it to the genome
   sequence, once per annotation;
2. `RiboseQC_analysis()`: analyse one or more BAM files with this annotation.

Then it shows some of the results, with the functions that make the plots of
the HTML report.

```{r load_lib, message = FALSE}
library(RiboseQC)
```


## Example data

The example data are Ribo-seq reads from roots and shoots of *Arabidopsis
thaliana* [3], on 309 genes: 99 on the five nuclear chromosomes, 88 on the
chloroplast genome (`ChrC`) and 122 on the mitochondrial genome (`ChrM`).

- `simp_arab.gtf.gz`: the annotation of these genes, from Araport11 [4];
- `simp_arab.fa.gz`: the genome sequence (TAIR10 [5]), with the bases away
  from these genes replaced by N (99.6% of the genome);
- `simp_arab_root.bam` and `simp_arab_shoots.bam`: the Ribo-seq reads of a
  root and a shoot sample, aligned to the genome, with their indexes;
- `root_results_RiboseQC`: the results of an earlier analysis of the root
  sample, which the examples of the help pages use.

```{r example_data}
ext_data <- system.file("ext_data", package = "RiboseQC")
list.files(ext_data)
```

All output files go to a temporary directory:

```{r out_dir}
out_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "RiboseQC_example")
dir.create(out_dir)
```


## Prepare the annotation

`prepare_annotation_files()` reads a GTF file and the genome sequence, and
writes a *TxDb* and an `_Rannot` file to `annotation_directory`. The `_Rannot`
file holds the annotated features (transcripts, exons, CDS, UTRs, introns,
start and stop codons, ...) that `RiboseQC_analysis()` uses, and refers to the
genome sequence by its path. The genome sequence must be a FASTA file that
*Rsamtools* can read; the example one is compressed with gzip, so we write an
uncompressed copy first.

```{r prepare_annotation, results = "hide", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
genome_fasta <- file.path(out_dir, "simp_arab.fa")
Biostrings::writeXStringSet(Biostrings::readDNAStringSet(file.path(ext_data, "simp_arab.fa.gz")),
                            genome_fasta)
annotation_file <- prepare_annotation_files(annotation_directory = out_dir,
                                            gtf_file = file.path(ext_data, "simp_arab.gtf.gz"),
                                            genome_seq = genome_fasta)
```

(*txdbmaker* warns that some CDS phases are missing and that the *TxDb* has no
genome version; *RiboseQC* uses neither.)

`load_annotation()` loads the annotation into two variables of the environment
that calls it: `GTF_annotation`, a list of the annotated features, and
`genome_seq`, the genome sequence. `RiboseQC_analysis()` loads the annotation
itself; here we only look at it. The chloroplast and mitochondrial genomes are
circular, and each circular chromosome is a compartment of its own in the
analysis. `genetic_codes` gives the genetic code of each chromosome, here the
standard code (`1`) for all:

```{r load_annotation, message = FALSE}
load_annotation(annotation_file)
GTF_annotation$genetic_codes
```


## Analyse the BAM files

`RiboseQC_analysis()` reads each BAM file in chunks of `chunk_size` alignments
(with `n_cores` above 1, it analyses the chunks in parallel), and writes its
output files with the prefix given in `dest_names`. Then, with
`create_report = TRUE` (the default), it creates one HTML report of all
samples. The report includes all plots, so it is large (about 60 MB for these
two samples); here we create no report.

```{r analysis, results = "hide", message = FALSE}
RiboseQC_analysis(annotation_file = annotation_file,
                  bam_files = file.path(ext_data, c("simp_arab_root.bam", "simp_arab_shoots.bam")),
                  dest_names = file.path(out_dir, c("root", "shoots")),
                  sample_names = c("root", "shoots"),
                  create_report = FALSE)
```

```{r output_files}
list.files(out_dir, pattern = "^(root|shoots)_")
```

`<dest_name>_results_RiboseQC_all` holds all results, in the list `res_all`;
the *Details* section of `?RiboseQC_analysis` describes its elements.
`<dest_name>_results_RiboseQC` is a smaller copy of it, without the P-sites,
which the HTML report uses, and so do we here:

```{r load_results}
root <- get(load(file.path(out_dir, "root_results_RiboseQC")))
shoots <- get(load(file.path(out_dir, "shoots_results_RiboseQC")))
names(shoots)
```


## Read lengths and compartments

`read_stats$positions` counts the reads in each genomic region and compartment.
As expected for green tissue, the shoot sample has many more reads on the
chloroplast genome than the root sample:

```{r compartments}
sapply(list(root = root, shoots = shoots), function(x) colSums(x$read_stats$positions))
shoots$read_stats$positions
```

Most reads of the organelles are on CDS. The example BAM files also have reads
outside the 309 genes of the example annotation, so here many reads of the
nuclear genome are intergenic.

The plot functions of the report draw the same data. (They use the `size`
aesthetic for lines, which *ggplot2* 3.4.0 deprecated; this vignette hides
these warnings.) The read length distribution of each compartment shows that
the chloroplast ribosomes protect fragments of more lengths than the
cytoplasmic ribosomes (`nucl`):

```{r read_lengths, results = "hide", warning = FALSE, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5, out.width = "100%"}
plot_read_length_dist(shoots$read_stats$rld, "shoots")
```


## P-site offsets

For each compartment and read length, `RiboseQC_analysis()` calculates the
P-site offset (`cutoff`, the distance of the P-site from the read's 5' end)
from the 5' ends of the reads around start codons. Then it selects the read
lengths with in-frame signal, as `readlength_choice_method` says (by default
`"max_coverage"`). `<dest_name>_P_sites_offsets.tsv` has the offsets of the
selected read lengths, which it used for the P-sites:

```{r offsets}
read.delim(file.path(out_dir, "root_P_sites_offsets.tsv"))
read.delim(file.path(out_dir, "shoots_P_sites_offsets.tsv"))
```

In both samples, the 28-nt reads of the cytoplasmic ribosomes have the offset
12. In the shoot sample, 9 read lengths of the chloroplast are selected too. No
read length of the mitochondrion is selected, in either sample.
`<dest_name>_P_sites_calcs` has more data on each read length, such as its
frame preference, its percentage of the reads of its compartment (`pct_map`),
and for each method of `readlength_choice_method` if it selects the read
length. Some of its columns:

```{r calcs}
calcs <- read.delim(file.path(out_dir, "shoots_P_sites_calcs"))
calcs[, c("comp", "read_length", "cutoff", "frame_preference", "pct_map", "max_coverage")]
```

The 5' ends of the 28-nt reads are mostly in one frame of the CDS:

```{r frames, results = "hide", warning = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
plot_frame_dist_boxplot(shoots$selection_cutoffs$analysis_frame_cutoff, "nucl", "shoots")
```

So their P-sites show the reading frame. Here are the P-sites of the 28-nt
reads around the start and stop codons of the nuclear genes, coloured by
their frame:

```{r metagene, results = "hide", warning = FALSE, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5, out.width = "100%"}
psites_nucl <- get_metagene_data(shoots, "profiles_P_sites", "P_sites_subcodon", "nucl")
plot_metagene_bar(psites_nucl, "28", "shoots")
```


## The HTML report

`create_html_report()` creates the report from the `_results_RiboseQC` files
of one or more samples; `RiboseQC_analysis()` calls it with
`create_report = TRUE`. It needs [pandoc](https://pandoc.org):

```{r report, eval = FALSE}
create_html_report(input_files = file.path(out_dir, c("root_results_RiboseQC", "shoots_results_RiboseQC")),
                   input_sample_names = c("root", "shoots"),
                   output_file = file.path(out_dir, "report.html"))
```

It also saves each plot as an R object in `<output_file>_plots/rds/`;
`create_pdfs_from_rds_objects()` makes PDF files of them (`RiboseQC_analysis()`
does this with `pdf_plots = TRUE`).


## P-sites for ORFquant

*ORFquant* [6] finds and quantifies translated ORFs. It reads the P-sites and
the junction reads of a sample from `<dest_name>_for_ORFquant`.
`prepare_for_ORFquant()` creates the same file from a BAM file and the offsets
in `<dest_name>_P_sites_offsets.tsv`:

```{r for_orfquant, results = "hide", message = FALSE}
prepare_for_ORFquant(annotation_file = annotation_file,
                     bam_file = file.path(ext_data, "simp_arab_shoots.bam"),
                     path_to_rl_cutoff_file = file.path(out_dir, "shoots_P_sites_offsets.tsv"),
                     dest_name = file.path(out_dir, "shoots_prepared"))
```

```{r compare_for_orfquant}
from_analysis <- get(load(file.path(out_dir, "shoots_for_ORFquant")))
from_prepare <- get(load(file.path(out_dir, "shoots_prepared_for_ORFquant")))
names(from_analysis)
all.equal(from_analysis, from_prepare)
```


## Running RiboseQC on your own data

Your data need:

- a GTF file with `exon` and `CDS` lines, each with `transcript_id` and
  `gene_id`;
- the genome sequence as an uncompressed FASTA file, with the same chromosome
  names as the GTF and the BAM files. Give its absolute path: the `_Rannot`
  file refers to it by the path that you give;
- the Ribo-seq reads aligned to the genome (not to the transcriptome) with a
  spliced aligner such as STAR, sorted by coordinate and indexed with
  `samtools index`.

The [README](https://github.com/katarinagresova/RiboseQC#readme) describes the
input and output files. A whole genome takes much longer than this example;
`n_cores` above 1 analyses the chunks of a BAM file in forked processes, on
Linux or macOS. Without `dest_names`, the output files go next to the BAM
files.


## References

1. Ingolia NT, Ghaemmaghami S, Newman JRS, Weissman JS (2009). Genome-wide
   analysis in vivo of translation with nucleotide resolution using ribosome
   profiling. *Science* 324, 218–223.
2. Calviello L, Sydow D, Harnett D, Ohler U (2019). Ribo-seQC: comprehensive
   analysis of cytoplasmic and organellar ribosome profiling data. *bioRxiv*
   601468.
3. Hsu PY, Calviello L, Wu HL, Li FW, Rothfels CJ, Ohler U, Benfey PN (2016).
   Super-resolution ribosome profiling reveals unannotated translation events
   in *Arabidopsis*. *PNAS* 113, E7126–E7135.
4. Cheng CY, Krishnakumar V, Chan AP, Thibaud-Nissen F, Schobel S, Town CD
   (2017). Araport11: a complete reannotation of the *Arabidopsis thaliana*
   reference genome. *The Plant Journal* 89, 789–804.
5. Lamesch P et al. (2012). The Arabidopsis Information Resource (TAIR):
   improved gene annotation and new tools. *Nucleic Acids Research* 40,
   D1202–D1210.
6. Calviello L, Hirsekorn A, Ohler U (2020). Quantification of translation
   uncovers the functions of the alternative transcriptome. *Nature
   Structural & Molecular Biology* 27, 717–725.
